chapter_theme: The two princes are shown the country and the city on the road, ride into Podanam by night amid the king's army, bow before the king who embraces them, and are asked by him about the forest dust in their hair, which Vijayan answers with a lion's ravage and Tivittan joins in.

cast.role: an unnamed speaker who shows the sights of the road and city to one hearer, 804 to 813
the elder prince, who answers the king
the younger prince, who speaks in 825
the two princes, Vijayan and Tivittan
the king of Podanam who receives his sons
the king's army that rides out to meet the princes
the maidens who hold lamps and bow to the princes
the fierce lion that came to ruin the king's forest

804.reading: The speaker points out honey dripping from the tips of young plantains and the shed buds of jasmine falling among the cool lotuses of the ponds.
804.nuance: The verses 804 to 813 point at things to look at (காண், கேள்) and are taken as the speech of an unnamed guide to one hearer (814 says it was told to 'him'); the Tamil does not name speaker or hearer. The yamaka word play and run-together words make the exact picture doubtful.

805.reading: The speaker points to lilies and lotus blooms among the paddy, the lotus flowers shaming a smile.
805.nuance: The grammar of lines 1 to 3 is broken by the word division; only the lotuses that outdo a smile are sure.

806.reading: The speaker shows the smoke of boiling sugar-cane juice rising and mixing with the high groves nearby, so that the place looks like a mountain with clouds.
806.nuance: The cane-boiling smoke is the one concrete sign of the countryside's work; the rest of the verse is simile.

807.reading: The verse describes a woman whose cheek, eyes and dark hair carry the dark-blue lily and the sheen of sapphire.
807.nuance: The repeated word கருநீல is the poet's play on sound; whether the woman is a particular one or a type of the country women is not shown.

808.reading: The verse describes a woman's forehead, lips, bangles and hair against the flowering செங்கிடை plants of the fields.
808.nuance: The repeated word வளர்செங்கிடை and the compressed syntax leave both the plant and the sense of each line uncertain.

809.reading: The verse describes a woman dressed in leaves and garlanded with the flowers of the water lily, set in a field rich with them.
809.nuance: The refrain வயலாம்பல் is word play and the clauses are hard to attach to a subject.

810.reading: The verse pictures a woman of the grove, in a place thick with lotus petals, gladdened as if by the blooming lotus.
810.nuance: The refrain வளர்தாமரையல்லி is word play; the sense is only roughly fixed.

811.reading: The speaker bids a hearer listen to what rises as a woman of shining hair, in search of fame, lets fruit and honey run.
811.nuance: The words ஒருமாதவளும் and கிளர்பார்வையுற are corrupt or obscure, and the verse's subject is not clear.

812.reading: The speaker shows the gem-lit city rising, its wall tops, tower tops and flags blending with the sun's rays.
812.nuance: From here to 813 the guide turns from the country to the city ahead, which sets up the arrival in 814.

813.reading: The speaker shows the altars of the city's sacrificers, where the smoke of the oblations of righteous Vedic brahmins rises over the groves.
813.nuance: The poet lets the Jain epic's own travellers see Vedic fire-offerings as a mark of a well-ordered city; he gives no view of the rite itself.

814.reading: The speaker's telling ends as the princes come to the golden city at nightfall, while the city sounds, and their want is gone.
814.nuance: வறுமை நீங்கினார் is taken as the end of the road's hardship; the line does not say whose want or of what kind.
814.event: The two princes reach the king's city, Podanam, at nightfall.

815.reading: The king's wide army of young elephants and bridled horses comes in a ring of dust to circle the princes, its extent beyond measure.
815.nuance: The verse says 'we could not measure' (அளந்தறிந்திலம்), a poet's voice in the plural that is not a character's.
815.event: The king's army rides out and circles the princes to bring them in.

816.reading: The princes appear in the king's golden city like a creeper of red flowers in a wood, while maidens hold lamps in their hands.
816.event: Maidens line the way with hand-lamps as the princes ride into the city.

817.reading: The poet describes the city's high houses, dim with the smoke of perfumes, as if they were hills of cool snow.
817.nuance: The simile of snow mountains is the poet's only comment; no person acts.

818.reading: The poet describes the city at night, the rays of the young moon falling on garlands and ornaments as if the ancient city slept.
818.nuance: The jasmine garlands and the moon-lit gems carry the sleep image; no event is given.

819.reading: As the princes reach the palace, maidens bow at their feet and the king in his gem crown bids the youths come in.
819.nuance: The words நம்பிமார் வருக are the king's, in the poet's telling.
819.event: The king orders the princes brought before him in the palace.

820.reading: The princes, afraid of what the king will do, bow so that their locks touch his feet while he stands uneasy at heart.
820.nuance: The verse says the princes fear (அஞ்சி) and the king's heart is bewildered (மருளுறு). It does not say why, so the setting is probably that the king had been anxious about them.
820.event: The princes bow low to the king, who is troubled in mind.

821.reading: The king calls both strong-armed sons to him and holds them close with both his arms.
821.nuance: Line 1 and 2 hold what look like slips of the text (சிழ்ருவர், களிதல்); the embrace itself is clear.
821.event: The king calls the two princes forward and embraces them both.

822.reading: The king looks gladly at his sons as the dust of forest flowers falls from their hair.
822.nuance: The pollen from the forest is the first sign, which 823 turns into a question, that the princes have been in the wild.
822.event: The king, glad, sees flower pollen from the forest fall from the princes' hair.

823.reading: The king asks why the dust of forest blooms clings in the hair of the two, and Vijayan replies.
823.nuance: The question itself is carried in lines 1 to 3 in broken syntax; its sense is taken from what Vijayan answers.
823.event: The king asks how forest dust came into the princes' hair, and Vijayan answers.

824.reading: Vijayan says a fierce lion came to ruin the forest round about the city's edge, and that when it was reported, this mighty servant drove it away.
824.nuance: The words வேற்றுவன் தமர்கள் and இவ்வாற்றல்சால் அடியன் are obscure; the verse is read as Vijayan crediting his brother (the 'mighty servant') with removing the lion, which 825 appears to support, but the Tamil of 824 does not name him.
824.event: Vijayan reports to the king that a lion had come to ravage the forest and was removed.

825.reading: Tivittan adds that he too went with him to the mountain side, and the king's life flowers back as he hears it.
825.nuance: The speaker is named only as 'the son of the garlanded lord' (சிறுவன்), taken as the younger prince; the verse leaves open what exactly the lion's end was.
825.event: Tivittan tells the king he went along too, and the king is gladdened.

826.reading: By the king's order the youths in their anklets reach their lodging behind the long gate under the sun-lit tower.
826.nuance: This closes the sarukkam; the last line's words பள்ளி பம்பலங்கள் are obscure and are taken as their resting place.
826.event: On the king's order the princes go to their lodging in the palace.

links.note: Kural 65 says touching one's children is joy to the body; the king here holds both sons in both arms as soon as he sees them.
links.teaches: The king's embrace shows a father's bodily joy in his sons coming before any royal question.

gains.a: The verse gives the embrace but not why it is joy, which the couplet names as the pleasure of touch.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a scene of a king, who must rule, undone by the sight of his sons safe.

links.note: Kural 65 also names the joy of hearing children's words; in 825 the king revives when his son tells him he went along.
links.teaches: The king's lifting at his son's words gives the couplet's pleasure of the ear a sudden effect on life itself.

gains.a: The verse lacks a general statement that a child's speech alone can be a parent's joy.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where those words carry news of a danger passed, so joy follows relief.

links.note: Kural 550 likens the king's removal of the cruel to weeding a crop; 824 gives a lion ruining the king's forest, removed by his sons.
links.teaches: A king's clearing of harm to his land can be done by a beast-slaying prince, which widens the weeding image beyond wrongdoers.

gains.a: The verse lacks any rule that makes the removal of the menace the king's own charge, which the couplet supplies.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a menace that is a beast and not a criminal, and a son who acts for the king.

source_issues: Verses 804 to 813: the speaker, hearer and sense of the descriptive verses are inferred; the yamaka word play and run-together words hide the syntax of 805 and 807 to 811.
Verse 821 line 1 has சிழ்ருவர் and line 2 களிதல், slips for words not recoverable from the text alone.
Verse 824 line 3 வேற்றுவன் தமர்கள் is obscure, and 811 ஒருமாதவளும் is doubtful.
